items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: Does the gender pay gap extend to AI? New research finds female AI agents ‘paid’ less
items.content:
image:  Dr Mary Hausfeld, Assistant Professor, Kemmy Business School, University of Limerick

Credit: Alan Place/University of Limerick

New research from University of Limerick has found gender bias in the workplace could be replicated in interactions with artificial intelligence.

The study, co-authored by Dr Mary Hausfeld of UL's Kemmy Business School, examined whether the way Artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are presented influences how people treat them in a workplace setting.

Researchers placed 189 workers in a virtual reality office and asked them to complete work-related tasks with different AI assistants, including human-like agents presented with either male or female appearance.

Participants were then given real money to divide between themselves and the AI assistant for completing the tasks, allowing the researchers to recreate a real-world transaction and examine how much people were willing to pay AI for its work.

AI agents with a female appearance were paid less than their male-presenting counterparts, despite using the same underlying technology, according to the research.

The AI agents had the same underlying capabilities, yet participants treated them differently depending on how they were presented.

The male-presenting AI agent, 'Johan', received higher monetary rewards than the female-presenting agent, 'Johanna', while it was also perceived as more human-like.

Specifically, Johanna was paid 10.25% less than Johan for completing the same work.

The findings suggest that gender biases familiar from human workplaces could be reproduced in interactions with artificial intelligence, even when there is no difference in the technology.

Dr Hausfeld said the results raise important questions as AI agents increasingly become part of people's working lives.

“What is striking about our findings is that the technology behind these AI agents was exactly the same, but people did not treat them in the same way.

“We often think of AI as being neutral, but the way we design and present these systems can activate those same assumptions and biases that exist in our interactions with other people.

“As AI agents become more common in the workplace, we need to think carefully about the characteristics we give them and the behaviours those choices may encourage. We don't want to inadvertently reproduce existing inequalities in a new technological setting.”

The gender finding was part of a broader investigation into how the human-like appearance of AI influences workplace interactions.

Participants in the study worked with a text-based chatbot, a desk robot, and human-like AI agents. Although the systems were powered by the same underlying AI, participants trusted the human-like assistants more and gave them more credit for their contribution than the robot.

The researchers also discovered a significant gap between what participants said influenced them and how they actually behaved.

Many participants said they preferred AI that was clearly non-human and most indicated that the gender of an AI assistant did not matter to them. However, their subsequent evaluations and reward decisions indicated that these design characteristics could still influence their behaviour.

Participants also suggested they had no preference for an AI with female or male attributes, but their behaviour told a different story.

The findings highlight an emerging challenge for organisations as AI develops from a tool employees use into increasingly human-like AI agents that can act as coworkers and collaborators.

Dr Hausfeld argues that choices around the appearance and presentation of AI agents should therefore not be regarded simply as aesthetic design decisions. "Such choices may affect how much people trust AI, how they judge its contribution, and even how they financially reward it."

items.title: OpenTPU – An open-source AI accelerator, developed by AI
items.content:
An open-source AI accelerator, developed by AI.

openTPU brings the lessons of auto-arch-tournament

to AI accelerators. It asks two questions: how far can AI agents go at hardware design, and can

they build the chip that runs their own inference?

otpu-chat running LFM2.5-230M on the FPGA card (left), with otpu-smi showing the card's

openTPU is also a learning project. The whole accelerator lives in one small monorepo that you

can read end to end: the hardware design (SystemVerilog), the instruction set, a bit-exact

simulator, a kernel language and its compiler, and the host software that drives a real PCIe

card. If you want to understand how an AI accelerator works, from a matmul in Python down to

the wires, this is a good place to start.

The design runs ten modern models with their real weights on an Inspur YPCB-00338 card

(Xilinx Kintex-7 xc7k480t, two DDR3 channels), and the card produces the same tokens as the

Measured on the card: the first three models on 2026-09-29 with the production image

deploy_champ_e698dcd7 . LFM2-2.6B, SmolLM3-3B and Phi-4-mini on 2026-09-30, and Qwen3.5-2B and

4B and Gemma 4 on 2026-10-01, with build B, deploy_fused133c_79c5707a , production since then.

Build B decodes LFM2-2.6B, SmolLM3 and Phi-4-mini 8-9% faster than e698dcd7 (Gemma 4 E2B 10%),

at 91-94% of the DRAM peak instead of 82-87%. Qwen3.5-4B's int8 image is over 4 GiB.

The image: main e698dcd at 133.33 MHz, one bitstream for all models. It has LiteDRAM

controllers calibrated by a small CPU inside the memory core, a four-column systolic matrix

unit and the stream engine ( docs/stream.md ). DDR3-1066, with a 17.1 GB/s

The host: the card sits in opentpu (Intel Core i7-4790).

Method, tools/qual/perf.py : decode is 64 greedy tokens after a 512-token prompt, with the

host's argmax in the loop (not streamed). "Device" counts only the cycles the accelerator runs;

"wall" adds the host. Prefill is the 512-token prompt, on the device.

DRAM traffic comes from the card's own counters while it runs.

Gemma 4 E2B keeps its per-layer embedding tables on the card (3.5-3.6 GiB images;

docs/gemma4.md ); in int8 it does not fit. It matches Hugging Face's greedy

tokens on three prompts with either head. E4B's table (2.95 GB) stays on the host, which

copies one 11 KB row into the card per token; its image is 3.96 GiB, int8 with the head and

the first 24 layers' down projections in 4-bit ( docs/gemma4_e4b.md ).

In the card's own decode loop (the card picking every token) Gemma 4 decodes faster: E2B

11.01 / 12.73 tok/s (int8 / 4-bit head), E4B 3.83 tok/s, on the device.

Every configuration matches the simulator token for token, per-position and with the

resident decode program. More detail in docs/board.md .

With the logits streamed back while the card runs ( tools/decode_profile.py , 96 tokens), 4-bit

prefill: 1.3x (Qwen3.5) to 2.0x (LFM2 4-bit) faster.

The earlier images and their numbers are in docs/board.md , section 5.

Psiphon says it has started planning a move out of Canada over Bill C-22

The provider warns the law would undermine its open-source trust

The bill has cleared the House of Commons and now faces Senate scrutiny

Psiphon has become the latest tech provider to threaten to leave Canada over Bill C-22, the government's contentious lawful access bill.

The Toronto-based company told The Globe and Mail it has started drawing up plans to move its operations out of the country. It says the bill would force it to compromise the safety features protecting users in authoritarian countries like Iran, Russia, and China.

Psiphon joins Signal, NordVPN , and Windscribe , all of which have warned they could pull out of Canada. For Canadians relying on the best VPN to protect their privacy, that list is getting uncomfortably long.

(Image credit: Future) NEW : Leave No Trace — A weekly newsletter on digital privacy and online surveillance.

Leave No Trace investigates the companies and governments putting our digital freedom at risk — and the people fighting back.

📩 Subscribe now to get every edition delivered to your inbox every Friday, launching this September.

Psiphon says open-source code can't hide a backdoor

Psiphon began as a Citizen Lab project at the University of Toronto in 2006 and now has around 20 million monthly users, many of whom rely on the tool to circumvent state censorship.

Unlike many VPN providers, Psiphon publishes all its code, but Bill C-22 could require it to change its systems to enable law enforcement's access, while keeping those changes secret.

Vice-president Kenzie Elsworthy said Psiphon is trusted thanks to the open-source model, and that it would be impossible to add a secret back door into a system that's completely public. "That is not lawful access . It is a published vulnerability," Elsworthy said.

Elsworthy stressed that the company doesn't want to leave, but if the law passes unchanged, relocating would be the only option. That would be awkward for Ottawa, which gave Psiphon about $600,000 in National Research Council funding this year.

Introduced on March 12, 2026, Bill C-22 would require telecoms, internet companies, and other electronic service providers to build surveillance capabilities for police and CSIS. Its backers argue Canada lags behind its Five Eyes allies without such powers.

The definition of "electronic service provider" is broad enough to cover messaging apps and VPNs. The government amended the bill before it passed the House on June 18, adding protections for end-to-end encryption and cutting metadata retention to six months instead of a year. It now heads to the Senate.

Tech companies are preparing for the worst

Because the bill won't define exactly who faces obligations until after it passes, all "ESP" companies are being forced to prepare for the worst.

Last month, 23 companies, including Windscribe, Nord Security, and ExpressVPN's parent company Kape Technologies, urged the government to fix the bill . Citizen Lab founder Ron Deibert warned that, as written, it would make it impossible for many vital privacy tools to operate in Canada.

With the Senate now in charge and European privacy groups also raising concerns, Psiphon's warning is hard to ignore.
